{{Short description|Type of mathematical group}}
{{More citations needed|date=March 2023}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[group theory]], a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] ''G'' is '''residually finite''' or '''finitely approximable''' if for every element ''g'' that is not the identity in ''G''  there is a [[Group homomorphism|homomorphism]] ''h'' from ''G'' to a [[finite group]], such that <math>h(g) \neq 1.\,</math>{{sfn|Magnus|p=306}}

There are a number of equivalent definitions:
*A group is residually finite if for each non-identity element in the group, there is a [[normal subgroup]] of finite [[index (group theory)|index]] not containing that element.
*A group is residually finite if and only if the intersection of all its [[subgroup]]s of finite index is [[trivial group|trivial]].  
*A group is residually finite if and only if the intersection of all its normal subgroups of finite index is trivial.
*A group is residually finite if and only if it can be embedded inside the [[direct product of groups|direct product]] of a family of finite groups.

== Definition ==

A [[Group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> is residually finite if, for every <math>1_G \neq g \in G</math>{{efn|where <math>1_G</math> denotes the [[identity element]] of the group <math>G</math>}}, there exists some [[finite group]] <math>F</math> and some [[group homomorphism]] <math>\phi : G \to F </math> such that <math>\phi(g) \neq 1_F</math>.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=61|loc=Definition 2.1.1}} There are other equivalent characterizations of residually finite groups:
* A group <math>G</math> is residually finite if and only if, for every <math>g, h \in G</math> where <math>g \neq h</math>, there exists some finite group <math>F</math> and some group homomorphism <math>\phi : G \to F </math> such that <math>\phi(g) \neq \phi(h)</math>.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=62|loc=Proposition 2.1.2}}
* A group is residually finite if and only if its [[residual subgroup]] (or profinite kernel) is trivial. The residual subgroup of a group is the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of all [[subgroups]] that have a [[finite index]], or equivalently, the intersection of all [[normal subgroups]] of finite index.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=63|loc=Proposition 2.1.11}}
* A group is residually finite if and only if it is [[isomorphic]] to a subgroup of a [[direct product]] of a family of finite groups.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=64|loc=Corollary 2.2.6}}

== Examples ==

Every finite group is residually finite. This can be shown by considering the group itself as the finite group, and its identity homomorphism as the homomorphism to a finite group.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=62|loc=Proposition 2.1.3}}

The [[integers]] are an example of an [[infinite group|infinite]] residually finite group. Given any non-zero integer <math>k</math> and letting <math>m</math> be an integer with <math>m > |k|</math>, the canonical homomorphism from the integers to the group of integers modulo <math>m</math>, <math>\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z} </math>, does not map <math>k</math> onto <math>0</math>.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=62|loc=Proposition 2.1.4}} a similar technique done on the entries of the matrices of <math>GL_n(\mathbb{Z})</math>, for <math>n \geq 1</math>, shows that this group is also residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=62|loc=Proposition 2.1.5}} More generally, all [[finitely generated abelian groups]] are residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=64|loc=Corollary 2.2.4}} Furthermore, the [[automorphism group]] of any finitely generated residually finite group will be residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=69|loc=Theorem 2.5.1}}

Subgroups of a residually finite group are themselves residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=64|loc=Proposition 2.2.1}} The direct product{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=64|loc=Proposition 2.2.2}} and direct sum{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=64|loc=Corollary 2.2.3}} of residually finite groups will also be residually finite.

Any [[inverse limit]] of residually finite groups is residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=65|loc=Proposition 2.2.7}} In particular, all [[profinite group]]s are residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=65|loc=Corollary 2.2.8}} One example of a profinite group is the [[p-adic integers]].{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=65|loc=Example 2.2.9}}

If a group has a subgroup of finite index which is residually finite (that is, a [[virtually]] residually finite group), then said group is also residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=65|loc=Lemma 2.2.11}}

More examples of groups that are residually finite are [[free group]]s{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=66|loc=Theorem 2.3.1}}, [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] [[nilpotent group]]s, [[polycyclic group]]s{{sfn|Magnus|p=310}}, [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] [[General linear group|linear groups]]{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=75|loc=Notes}}, and [[fundamental group]]s of compact [[3-manifold]]s<ref>https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781400882083-018/html</ref>.

=== Nonexamples ===

A [[divisible group]] is a group <math>G</math> where every <math>g \in G</math> and integer <math>n \geq 1</math> has an element <math>h \in G</math> where <math>h^n = g</math>. Examples of nontrivial divisible groups include the [[rational numbers]], the [[real numbers]], the [[complex numbers]], the [[additive group]] of a [[vector space]] over the rationals, and the additive group of every field with [[characteristic (field theory)|characteristic]] 0.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=62|loc=Example 2.1.5}} Every nontrivial divisible group fails to be residually finite as every homomorphism from a divisible group to a finite group is trivial.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=62|loc=Lemma 2.1.7, Proposition 2.1.8}}

Examples of non-residually finite groups can be constructed using the fact that all finitely generated residually finite groups are [[Hopfian group]]s{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=68|loc=Theorem 2.4.3}}. For example the [[Baumslag–Solitar group]] <math>B(1,m)</math> for <math>|m| \geq 2</math> is finitely generated, residually finite, and Hopfian{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=79|loc=Exercise 2.13}}
, but <math>B(2,3)</math> is finitely generated yet not Hopfian, and therefore not residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=80|loc=Exercise 2.14}}

Every infinite [[simple group]] is not residually finite because the only normal subgroup with a finite index will be the group itself.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=71|loc=Lemma 2.6.2}} This implies that the [[Symmetric group|group of permutations]] on an infinite set with [[finite support]] is not residually finite as the subgroup with the permutations of signature 1 is an infinite simple group.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=71|loc=Lemma 2.6.3}} This can be used to show that the subgroup of permutation on the integers generated by the translation <math>n \mapsto n+1</math> and the transposition of <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> is a finitely generated Hopfian group that is not residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=71|loc=Lemma 2.6.1}}

[[Group extension]]s of residually finite groups also need not be residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=73|loc=Remark 2.6.6}} One counter example is the [[wreath product]] of <math>A_5</math>, the [[alternating group]] of degree 5, with the integers, both of which are residually finite.{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=73|loc=Proposition 2.6.5}}

== Properties ==

Finitely presented residually finite groups have a solvable [[word problem for groups|word problem]]{{sfn|Magnus|p=307}}, meaning there is a procedure where, given the group's generators, one can find the words that equate to the identity element{{sfn|Magnus|p=305}}.

== Topology ==

Every group ''G'' may be made into a [[topological group]] by taking as a [[basis of open neighbourhoods]] of the identity, the collection of all normal subgroups of finite index in ''G''.  The resulting [[topology]] is called the [[profinite group|profinite topology]] on ''G''{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=77|loc=Exercise 2.5.a, 2.5.c}}.  A group is residually finite if, and only if, its profinite topology is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]].{{sfn|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|p=77|loc=Exercise 2.5.e}} If this group is also infinite and finitely generated, then said topology is [[totally disconnected]], and the [[completion (topology)|completion]] is the inverse limit of a sequence of finite quotients of this group, making it a profinite group.{{sfn|Magnus|p=307}}

A group whose [[cyclic subgroup]]s are closed in the profinite topology is said to be <math>\Pi_C\,</math>.
Groups each of whose finitely generated subgroups are closed in the profinite topology are called '''subgroup separable''' (also '''LERF''', for ''locally extended residually finite'').
A group in which every [[conjugacy class]] is closed in the profinite topology is called '''conjugacy separable'''.{{cn|date=December 2025}}

== Varieties of residually finite groups ==

One question is: what are the properties of a [[variety (universal algebra)|variety]] all of whose groups are residually finite? Two results about these are:

* Any variety comprising only residually finite groups is generated by an [[A-group]].{{cn|date=December 2025}}
* For any variety comprising only residually finite groups, it contains a finite group such that all members are embedded in a direct product of that finite group.{{cn|date=December 2025}}
